body:
Understanding river geography

A river flows from its source towards its mouth under the influence of gravity. Its source may be a glacier, spring, lake or upland region. Its mouth is where it discharges into another water body.

A tributary joins a larger river, while a distributary branches away from it. The land area drained by a river and its tributaries forms a drainage basin.

In world map questions, a river's location is often established by its source region, the countries through which it passes and the sea or lake into which it ultimately drains.

Rivers of eastern and southeastern Asia

RiverPrincipal geographical regionMouth
Yangtze or Chang JiangChinaEast China Sea
Yellow River or Huang HeNorthern ChinaBohai Sea
MekongChina and mainland Southeast AsiaSouth China Sea
Irrawaddy or AyeyarwadyMyanmarAndaman Sea
SalweenChina, Myanmar and part of the Thailand-Myanmar borderAndaman Sea
Chao PhrayaThailandGulf of Thailand
AmurRussia-China border region and Russian Far EastWaters between the Russian mainland and Sakhalin

The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia. Both the Yangtze and Yellow River flow generally eastward across China, but they reach different coastal water bodies.

The Mekong passes through or along the borders of 6 countries: China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam. Its delta lies mainly in southern Vietnam.

The Irrawaddy is the principal river system of Myanmar. The Chao Phraya flows through central Thailand, including Bangkok.

Rivers of northern Asia

The Ob, Yenisei and Lena rivers are prominent rivers of Siberia. Their general flow is northward towards the Arctic Ocean.

RiverReceiving water body
Ob-Irtysh systemKara Sea
YeniseiKara Sea
LenaLaptev Sea

From west to east, their approximate geographical order is Ob, Yenisei and Lena. Their northward drainage distinguishes them from the major eastward-flowing rivers of China.

Rivers of southern and western Asia

RiverPrincipal geographical regionMouth
IndusTibetan region, India and PakistanArabian Sea
GangaIndia and BangladeshBay of Bengal through the combined delta system
BrahmaputraTibet, India and BangladeshBay of Bengal through the combined delta system
TigrisTürkiye and IraqPersian Gulf through the Shatt al-Arab
EuphratesTürkiye, Syria and IraqPersian Gulf through the Shatt al-Arab
JordanJordan Rift ValleyDead Sea

The Tigris and Euphrates are closely associated with Mesopotamia, the historical region between the two rivers. They join in southern Iraq to form the Shatt al-Arab waterway.

The Brahmaputra is known as the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet, the Siang or Dihang in part of Arunachal Pradesh and the Jamuna in Bangladesh.

Inland drainage of Central Asia

Not every river reaches an ocean. An endorheic drainage basin is an inland drainage basin whose water has no natural outlet to the sea.

The Amu Darya and Syr Darya historically discharged into the Aral Sea. Large-scale diversion of their waters for irrigation contributed to the severe shrinkage of the Aral Sea.

Major rivers of Europe

RiverImportant geographical associationMouth
VolgaRussia; longest river in EuropeCaspian Sea
DanubeCentral and southeastern EuropeBlack Sea
RhineWestern EuropeNorth Sea
DnieperRussia, Belarus and UkraineBlack Sea
DonRussiaSea of Azov
ThamesEngland, including LondonNorth Sea
SeineFrance, including ParisEnglish Channel
PoNorthern ItalyAdriatic Sea
RhoneSwitzerland and FranceMediterranean Sea

The Danube flows generally eastward from Germany towards the Black Sea. Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade are national capitals situated along it.

The Volga terminates in the Caspian Sea rather than reaching the Black Sea or Arctic Ocean. The Rhine drains towards the North Sea through western Europe.

Prelims focus

  • Yangtze is the longest river in Asia; Volga is the longest river in Europe.
  • Danube drains into the Black Sea.
  • Volga drains into the Caspian Sea.
  • Mekong reaches the South China Sea through Vietnam.
  • Ob, Yenisei and Lena drain towards the Arctic Ocean.
  • Trap: The Don enters the Sea of Azov, not the Caspian Sea.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Environment, 2018–19, Human Environment Interactions: The Tropical and the Subtropical Region, pp. 56–60; NCERT, Class 12, Fundamentals of Human Geography, Transport and Communication, pp. 75–76; Orient BlackSwan School Atlas, World – Physical, Important Rivers, p. 81 and regional physical maps; Geogra, Physical Map of the World, river and drainage features; Riveryas, Atlas of the World's Rivers, based on RiverATLAS; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
title: Major Rivers of Asia and Europe

body:
The Nile and other African rivers

The major river systems of Africa drain into the Mediterranean Sea, Atlantic Ocean and Indian Ocean. Their courses are influenced by the continent's extensive plateaus, uplands and basins.

RiverPrincipal regionMouth
NileNortheastern AfricaMediterranean Sea
CongoCentral AfricaAtlantic Ocean
NigerWestern AfricaGulf of Guinea
ZambeziSouthern AfricaIndian Ocean
OrangeSouthern AfricaAtlantic Ocean
LimpopoSouthern AfricaIndian Ocean

The Nile river system

The Nile flows generally northward through northeastern Africa. Its 2 major branches, the White Nile and Blue Nile, meet at Khartoum in Sudan.

The White Nile is associated with the East African lake region, while the Blue Nile originates from Lake Tana in the Ethiopian Highlands. The combined Nile flows through Egypt before entering the Mediterranean Sea.

Other distinctive African river systems

The Congo River drains the equatorial region of Central Africa and crosses the Equator twice. Its enormous drainage basin supports extensive tropical rainforest.

The Niger follows a curved course through western Africa before reaching the Gulf of Guinea in Nigeria. The Niger River and the country of Niger should not be confused with Nigeria, where the river reaches the sea.

The Zambezi is associated with Victoria Falls, situated on the Zambia-Zimbabwe boundary. It reaches the Indian Ocean through Mozambique.

Major rivers of North America

RiverPrincipal geographical regionMouth
Mississippi-MissouriCentral United StatesGulf of Mexico
St. LawrenceCanada and the Great Lakes regionGulf of St. Lawrence and Atlantic Ocean
MackenzieNorthwestern CanadaBeaufort Sea, Arctic Ocean
YukonCanada and AlaskaBering Sea
ColoradoSouthwestern United States and MexicoGulf of California, its natural drainage destination
Rio GrandeUnited States-Mexico border regionGulf of Mexico
ColumbiaWestern Canada and northwestern United StatesPacific Ocean

The Mississippi-Missouri river system drains a vast part of central North America. The Colorado River is associated with the Grand Canyon. Its downstream flow has been heavily modified by dams and water withdrawals.

The Great Lakes

The 5 Great Lakes of North America are Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario. Their waters ultimately drain towards the Atlantic Ocean through the St. Lawrence River.

Lake Michigan is located entirely within the United States. The other 4 lakes are shared by the United States and Canada.

Niagara Falls is situated on the Niagara River between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario.

Major rivers of South America

River systemPrincipal geographical regionMouth
AmazonNorthern South AmericaAtlantic Ocean
OrinocoVenezuela and ColombiaAtlantic Ocean
Paraná-ParaguayCentral and southeastern South AmericaRío de la Plata estuary and Atlantic Ocean
UruguaySouthern Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina regionRío de la Plata estuary
São FranciscoBrazilAtlantic Ocean

The Amazon originates in the Andean region and flows generally eastward across South America. It has the largest drainage basin and greatest average water discharge of any river in the world.

The Nile is conventionally listed as the world's longest river. Some measurements propose a greater length for the Amazon because river length depends on the identification of the most distant source and the mouth. Therefore, length and discharge must be treated as different measures.

Australia's Murray-Darling system

The Murray and Darling rivers form the principal interconnected river system of southeastern Australia. The Darling joins the Murray, which reaches the Southern Ocean coastal waters near South Australia's Murray Mouth.

Waterfalls and river associations

WaterfallRiverLocation
Victoria FallsZambeziZambia-Zimbabwe boundary
Niagara FallsNiagaraCanada-United States boundary
Iguazu FallsIguazuArgentina-Brazil boundary
Angel FallsChurún River systemVenezuela

Prelims focus

  • The White Nile and Blue Nile meet at Khartoum.
  • The Congo River crosses the Equator twice.
  • Victoria Falls is associated with the Zambezi River.
  • The Mississippi-Missouri system drains into the Gulf of Mexico.
  • The Amazon has the world's largest drainage basin and greatest average discharge.
  • Trap: Lake Michigan is entirely within the United States, unlike the other 4 Great Lakes.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, The Earth: Our Habitat, 2018–19, Chapter 5, pp. 32–33; NCERT, Class 7, Our Environment, 2018–19, Amazon Basin, pp. 56–58; NCERT, Class 12, Fundamentals of Human Geography, Transport and Communication, pp. 75–76; Orient BlackSwan School Atlas, World – Physical, Important Rivers, p. 81 and regional physical maps; Geogra, Physical Map of the World; Riveryas, Atlas of the World's Rivers; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Major Rivers of Africa, the Americas and Australia

body:
What makes a region a desert?

A desert is a region of very low precipitation, generally receiving less than approximately 250 mm of precipitation annually. The precise boundary between desert and semi-desert conditions also depends on evaporation and the availability of moisture.

Deserts are defined primarily by aridity rather than high temperature. Some deserts experience extreme summer heat, while others remain cold for much of the year.

Antarctica is the world's largest desert when polar deserts are included. The Sahara is the world's largest hot desert.

Hot deserts of Africa and Asia

DesertLocationImportant characteristic
SaharaNorthern AfricaLargest hot desert
Arabian DesertArabian PeninsulaIncludes the Rub' al Khali sand desert
TharNorthwestern India and eastern PakistanHot subtropical desert
KalahariBotswana, Namibia and South AfricaExtensive sandy, largely semi-arid region
NamibSouthwestern African coast, mainly NamibiaCoastal desert influenced by the cold Benguela Current

The Sahara extends across northern Africa from the Atlantic coast towards the Red Sea region. Its southern margin gradually gives way to the Sahel, a semi-arid transitional zone between the desert and the wetter savanna regions farther south.

The Kalahari lies predominantly in the interior of southern Africa. The Namib occupies a narrow coastal region farther west. They differ in both geographical position and the nature of their aridity.

Cold and continental deserts of Asia

DesertLocation
GobiMongolia and northern China
TaklamakanTarim Basin, Xinjiang, western China
KarakumMainly Turkmenistan
KyzylkumMainly Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan
Ladakh cold desertHigh-altitude region of the northern Indian subcontinent

The Gobi and Taklamakan deserts experience cold winters. Their continental locations and surrounding mountain systems contribute to limited precipitation.

Ladakh lies in a high-altitude rain-shadow region. Its aridity is an example of how mountains can restrict the movement of moist air into an interior region.

Deserts of the Americas and Australia

DesertLocationCharacteristic
AtacamaMainly northern ChileExtremely arid Pacific coastal desert
PatagonianMainly southern ArgentinaCold rain-shadow desert east of the Andes
MojaveSouthwestern United StatesIncludes Death Valley
SonoranSouthwestern United States and northwestern MexicoHot desert
ChihuahuanNorthern Mexico and southwestern United StatesLarge interior desert
Great BasinWestern United StatesCold desert
Great VictoriaSouthern interior AustraliaMajor Australian desert
Great SandyNorthwestern AustraliaInterior sandy desert
SimpsonCentral AustraliaExtensive sand-dune desert

Why deserts occur in different geographical settings

Subtropical high-pressure regions

Many hot deserts occur near subtropical latitudes, commonly around 20° to 30° north or south. Descending air in subtropical high-pressure regions tends to suppress cloud formation and rainfall. The Sahara and Arabian deserts are prominent examples.

Cold ocean currents

The cold Peru or Humboldt Current contributes to the aridity of the Atacama Desert. The cold Benguela Current contributes to the aridity of the Namib Desert. Although nearby oceans supply atmospheric moisture, cool and stable coastal air often produces fog rather than substantial rainfall.

Rain shadows and continental interiors

When moist air rises over mountains, it cools and may produce precipitation on the windward side. Air descending on the leeward side becomes relatively warmer and drier. This can produce a rain-shadow desert, as in Patagonia east of the Andes.

Regions far from oceans also receive limited maritime moisture. Continental interiors and surrounding mountains help explain the aridity of several Central Asian deserts.

Polar deserts

Polar deserts receive very little precipitation because extremely cold air has a limited capacity to hold water vapour. Antarctica contains extensive ice accumulated over long periods, despite its low annual precipitation.

Gujarat's arid and saline landscapes

The Rann of Kachchh is a vast saline, seasonally inundated landscape in western India. It is associated with the arid northwestern region of the Indian subcontinent, but its salt-marsh environment differs from the extensive sand dunes characteristic of many hot deserts.

The Great Rann of Kachchh lies mainly north of the Kachchh mainland, while the Little Rann lies farther southeast.

Prelims focus

  • Sahara is the largest hot desert; Antarctica is the largest desert overall.
  • Gobi lies in Mongolia and China.
  • Taklamakan lies in western China.
  • Atacama is associated with the Humboldt Current.
  • Namib is associated with the Benguela Current.
  • Trap: Patagonia lies mainly east of the Andes in Argentina, whereas the Atacama lies mainly west of the Andes in Chile.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Environment, 2018–19, Life in the Deserts and Natural Vegetation and Wildlife; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Class 11, English-medium 2020 edition, Hydrosphere, pp. 90–93; Orient BlackSwan School Atlas, World – Physical, p. 81; NOAA, JetStream Max: Major Ocean Currents; ViewOurPlanet, World's Largest Deserts, geographical locations and desert classifications; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
